entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Constitution of the Empire of Japan, promulgated on February 11, 1889, marked a pivotal turn in Japan's political landscape and its engagement with the world, establishing a constitutional monarchy that sought to modernize and westernize the nation. Drafted under the guidance of influential figures such as Emperor Meiji and his advisors, including the statesman Ito Hirobumi, the constitution was a response to both domestic pressures for reform and external demands for equality from Western powers. This document not only signified Japan's transition from feudal rule to a more centralized governance structure but also reflected the broader global trend of constitutionalism in the late 19th century.

The constitution introduced a bicameral legislature known as the Imperial Diet, which consisted of the House of Peers and the House of Representatives, thus laying a foundation for representative governance in Japan. Although it granted certain rights to the populace, the emperor retained significant powers, including the ability to dissolve the Diet and command the military, which ultimately limited the democratic nature of the system. The document was also notable for its attempts to balance traditional Japanese values with the influences of Western political thought, encapsulating Japan's desire to assert itself as a modern state on the global stage.
